title: A projected gradient algorithm for solving the maxcut SDP relaxation
contribution: Solves the maxcut SDP by a projected gradient method on the lower-triangular factorization X = LL^T, faster and using less memory than Benson et al. and Homer-Peinado at moderate (0.2%) accuracy.
problem_entry: The Goemans-Williamson SDP step does not scale: Newton-based IPMs are expensive, and first-order methods win when only moderate accuracy is needed (p. 2).
key_idea: Restrict Homer-Peinado's factor to be lower triangular; projected gradient with row normalization and an Armijo search; a greedy vertex reordering lowers the per-iteration cost m(G) (pp. 5-13).
assumptions: Nonnegative weights for the 0.87856 guarantee; L may have a negative diagonal so there are no inequalities (chosen after limited testing, p. 5); no global-convergence theorem, and non-global limit points are called unlikely (p. 8).
proof_devices: Prop. 3.2: a dual slack S = Diag(lambda) - C >= 0 at a stationary point certifies global optimality, because SX is strictly upper triangular (p. 8)
Prop. 3.1: the projected gradient is zero iff the point is stationary, with explicit multipliers (p. 7)
flop counts in terms of the ordering measure m(G) (pp. 10-12)
Armijo trial steps cost O(|E|) via the quadratic-in-alpha expansion (7) (pp. 11-12)
the projected-gradient and unconstrained steepest-ascent directions coincide (p. 9)
experiments: 21-27 rudy G-set graphs, n = 800-7000; baselines byz (dual-scaling IPM) and Homer-Peinado, run with the authors' own codes; stop at 0.2% and 0.02% of a reference value solved to a 1e-6 gap; reports times, iterations, memory and the best of n random cuts; losses (weaker cuts, slow tail) printed (pp. 13-19).
positioning: A variant of Homer-Peinado, measured against Benson-Ye-Zhang; the comparison with Helmberg-Rendl's spectral bundle method is left open as unclear (pp. 2, 20).
writing: A running-theme sentence in the introduction, a three-point list of main conclusions before Section 2, and specific hedges on effects the authors cannot explain (pp. 2-3, 17).
limits_future: Slow asymptotic convergence and weaker cuts than the IPM; future work: parallelize, add second-order information, extend to other SDPs (pp. 17, 20).

method_links.note: A variant of an existing code, benchmarked against the best codes the authors could obtain; step size and stopping rule set by experiment; the global-convergence gap is stated.
The claim that iterates never converge to a non-global point is labelled as an observation (unlikely, always observed) and is not certified.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dual certificate for a factored nonconvex reformulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Prop. 3.2 builds the SDP dual slack from the stationarity multipliers of the factored problem and certifies global optimality when it is PSD.

transferable: Derive an a-posteriori global certificate S = Diag(lambda) - C >= 0 from the stationarity multipliers of a factored SDP (p. 8).
Express the per-iteration cost through a graph quantity, reorder the input to reduce it, and report the measured ratio (pp. 10-13).
Run every competitor to the same relative-error target, computed from a high-accuracy reference solve, at two accuracy levels (pp. 14-16).

quotes.text: a running theme of this paper is that the speed of first-order methods make them attractive choices for solving the maxcut SDP relaxation, particularly when one desires a solution of only moderate accuracy.
We currently are unable to give a reasonable explanation as to why this occurs

title: Rank-two relaxation heuristics for max-cut and other binary quadratic programs
contribution: Replaces the Goemans-Williamson SDP by a nonconvex rank-two (angular) relaxation and builds the code CirCut, which finds better cuts than SDP-based codes in a fraction of the time but gives no upper bound.
problem_entry: Asks whether GW-type SDP approaches can become competitive on large problems; answers no for lower bounds, because the SDP does not scale (p. 2).
key_idea: Unit vectors in R^2 instead of R^n give the unconstrained problem min f(theta) = 1/2 W.cos(T(theta)); a deterministic sweep over all half-circle cuts; the rounded cut (a saddle point) is perturbed and the search restarted (pp. 4-9).
assumptions: The relaxation is nonconvex with many local minima; the GW bound holds only relative to psi(theta), which is not an upper bound, so there is no performance guarantee (pp. 4-5, 8).
proof_devices: Prop. 3.1: every cut is a stationary point of f (p. 6)
Lemma 3.3: x is a maximum cut iff M(x) is nonnegatively summable, via q(x) - q(xbar) = 2 delta^T M delta (p. 6)
Theorem 3.4: the Hessian at a cut equals M(x); a cut that is a local minimum is a maximum cut, and all other cuts are saddle points (p. 7)
K3 counterexample to the converse (p. 7)
the GW analysis carried over to rank two: gamma(x*) >= 0.878 psi(theta) (p. 8)
experiments: CirCut (Fortran90, minimization stopped loosely at 1e-4) against SBmethod at default parameters on 4 DIMACS torus graphs; against DSDP times as reported by Choi-Ye on 27 G-set graphs up to n = 20000 (a different machine, with reasons given); against Hartmann's spin-glass heuristic on 20 cubic lattices; MAX-BISECTION on 13 graphs; losses (G50, Hartmann's H2) printed (pp. 9-17).
positioning: Builds on Goemans-Williamson but argues that the SDP relaxation holds little promise for producing lower bounds; warns that the SDP codes also give upper bounds (pp. 2, 9, 11, 18).
writing: A rhetorical question with a hedged partial answer, a paragraph giving the geometric interpretation, and numbered factors behind the performance (pp. 2, 9, 17).
limits_future: No upper bound; MIN-BISECTION with positive weights unresolved; carrying the method to other problems needs case-by-case study; MAX-CLIQUE named as the next candidate (pp. 1, 15, 17-18).

method_links.note: A known relaxation plus a rank restriction, implemented and benchmarked against the best public SDP codes at their default parameters; the missing guarantee is stated.

The direction is reversed: the paper leaves the convex lifted object for a nonconvex low-rank formulation, because the goal is primal solutions, not a bound. This contrasts with his later taste for a single strong bound.
No engineered hard pool: standard libraries plus an external physics family, with the family where CirCut loses kept in the tables.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: classify local optima of a continuous formulation combinatorially, then escape saddles
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 3.4 shows that cuts other than maximum cuts are saddle points of f; Algorithm 1 restarts from perturbed cuts.

transferable: Round exhaustively and deterministically at rank two: sort the angles and sweep all half-circle cuts (pp. 7-8).
Restart from a slight perturbation of the rounded discrete point, since the theory makes it a saddle point unless it is optimal (pp. 7-9).
When a competitor cannot be rerun, list the reasons and compare only where the gaps are orders of magnitude (p. 11).
Compute the relaxation's Hessian at discrete points and match it to a combinatorial optimality condition (pp. 6-7).

quotes.text: Since these codes produce both an upper bound and a lower bound, while our code only gives the latter, the comparisons should not be taken at face value.
CirCut does not seem to be able to achieve the same cut values as H2 even if CirCut is allowed to search for a very long time.

title: Solving a class of semidefinite programs via nonlinear programming
contribution: Turns a class of linear and nonlinear SDPs into NLPs over an orthant (a square-slack Cholesky substitution followed by an elimination), gives gradient formulas through a dual estimate, and proves global convergence of a first-order log-barrier method for linear SDPs.
problem_entry: Interior-point methods are limited at large scale by dense Newton systems; the goal is fewer constraints and methods that use only gradients (p. 2).
key_idea: Write S = LL^T, then eliminate the off-diagonal entries of L by a recursion in Cholesky order, so that the SDP becomes min f(L_I, y) over R^n_++ x R^N, a space whose dimension equals that of the feasible set (pp. 2, 6-9).
assumptions: The class NLSDP with D in I in K (maxcut, two Lovasz theta forms, PSD completion); for the algorithm, I = D, g linear, H affine, a strictly feasible dual and linear independence; the NLP generally has no optimal solution, because the optima lie on the boundary (pp. 4-5, 18).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: unique recursive elimination in Cholesky order (pp. 7-8)
Lemma 2 / Theorem 1: a homeomorphism between the orthant and int F_sdp, with equal optimal values (pp. 8-9)
Lemma 3 / Theorem 2: a dual estimate X, from a triangular linear system, gives the gradient 2 pi(XL) (pp. 9-11)
Lemma 5 / Theorem 5: dual feasibility and the duality gap are read off the gradient (p. 19)
Prop. 8 (a variant of Monteiro-Pang): level sets are compact (pp. 20-21)
Theorem 7: the transformed log-barrier problem has a unique stationary point, via XS = nu I, so the transformation adds no spurious stationary points (pp. 23-24)
flop and space counts for the dense, sparse and mixed cases (pp. 12-16)
experiments: none (numerics deferred to the companion reports [3] and [4], p. 25)
positioning: Follows Helmberg-Rendl, Homer-Peinado and Burer-Monteiro (S014); reads their substitutions as matrix square slacks and turns the known weakness of square slacks into a first step (pp. 2, 6).
writing: Admits heavy notation, tells the reader to assume the diagonal case, gives the main ideas before the formal statements, and uses five examples to show the scope (pp. 3-6).
limits_future: Convergence for nonlinear SDPs is harder; gradient methods give only moderate accuracy; generic NLP solvers are unlikely to work without exploiting structure; extensions are in companion papers (pp. 24-25).

method_links.note: An exact reformulation of the whole problem, with a bijection and equal optimal values, but into a nonconvex NLP over an orthant instead of a convex cone.
The theory paper comes first and the computation is split into companion reports; the maxcut prototype came earlier, in S014.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: dual certificate for a factored nonconvex reformulation
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The dual estimate X(w,y) yields the gradient, a dual-feasibility test and the duality gap; stationarity of the barrier problem maps to XS = nu I.

transferable: Follow a square-slack substitution with an elimination that leaves a simple orthant domain, and prove a bijection with the interior of the original feasible set (pp. 6-9).
Prove that the transformed barrier problem has a unique stationary point by mapping stationarity to XS = nu I; any convergent gradient method then suffices (pp. 23-24).
Define a dual estimate as the solution of a triangular system attached to the current factor, and read the gradient and dual feasibility from it (pp. 9-11, 19).

quotes.text: This paper is heavy in notation.

The square slack substitution is an old idea in nonlinear programming that has not been regarded as practically useful in general, in part because it can turn a convex feasibility set into a nonconvex one.

title: Maximum stable set formulations and heuristics based on continuous optimization
contribution: Shows that the rank-one and rank-two restrictions of the Lovasz theta SDP are exact nonconvex formulations of the stability number, classifies their local maxima, and builds escape-based heuristics (Max-AO) that find maximum stable sets on most DIMACS benchmarks.
problem_entry: Can the theta SDP give large stable sets without an SDP being solved? The strategy that worked for max-cut (S006) is carried over (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Restrict X to rank one and to rank two; both have optimal value alpha(G). At a stable set that is not maximum, the rank-two canonical points are not local maxima, so local search can escape. Rank three is not exact (pentagon) (pp. 4-13).
assumptions: Simple graphs; both NLPs are NP-hard, so only local solutions can be expected; the augmented Lagrangian converges to stationary points under mild conditions; escapes have no guarantee (pp. 1, 13, 15, 18).
proof_devices: Lemma 1: Cauchy-Schwarz gives (e^T x)^2 <= |S|, with equality only at the canonical vector (p. 4)
Theorem 2: the rank-one local maximizers are exactly the maximal stable sets, via an auxiliary problem restricted to the support (pp. 5-6)
Lemma 4: the support of a rank-two feasible point induces a bipartite subgraph (pp. 9-10)
Theorem 3(b): a chain of triangle, Pythagoras and Cauchy-Schwarz inequalities (9)-(13) (p. 9)
Lemma 5 / Prop. 1: a monotone feasible path between points along orthogonal directions shows that canonical points are not local maxima (pp. 11-12)
pentagon counterexample at rank three (p. 13)
Prop. 2: the support thresholded at eps^(1/2), B^I_z, is bipartite, so stable sets can be extracted from infeasible iterates (p. 16)
Appendix A: first-order conditions plus a contradiction by a rotated path (pp. 21-28); Appendix B: a local maximizer whose induced stable set is not maximal (pp. 28-29)
experiments: Max-AO (ANSI C; augmented Lagrangian with L-BFGS, a spherical line search and a tailored 0.01 stopping rule) on 64 DIMACS clique complements; three heuristics, ten runs each; success rates 42/65/75% on the 55 graphs with known alpha; the DIMACS machine-calibration benchmark; quality compared with Balas-Niehaus and Benson-Ye; the weak brock instances are named (pp. 15-21).
positioning: Extends the low-rank path of S006; credits Gruber-Rendl for alpha_1 = alpha(G); places itself in the continuous Motzkin-Straus line; keeps the value of the theta bound itself (pp. 3-4, 21).
writing: Announces a surprising result, uses a question as a section heading, recasts an apparent disadvantage as an advantage, and lists numbered claims in the overview (pp. 3, 6, 12-13).
limits_future: Rank-two local maxima are only partly characterized; escapes sometimes fail; weak on the brock instances; future work: the weighted case, a trust-region solver, hybrids with discrete heuristics, more reliable escapes (pp. 11, 18-19, 21).

method_links.note: Stops generalizing at the first rank where exactness fails and publishes the boundary with an explicit small counterexample (pentagon, rank three).
Keeps theory and observation apart (no theory for escapes; termination observed in practice) and states the incomplete classification, with a counterexample.
A strategy carried over from max-cut, prototyped with off-the-shelf NLP components; the adaptations are presented as open to improvement.
An exact reformulation of the whole problem, obtained by restricting the rank rather than by convexifying.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: classify local optima of a continuous formulation combinatorially, then escape saddles
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Rank-one local maxima are exactly the maximal stable sets; at a stable set that is not maximum, the rank-two canonical points are not local maxima; the heuristic restarts from perturbed canonical points.

transferable: Find the largest rank at which a low-rank restriction of an SDP stays exact, and certify failure at the next rank with the smallest counterexample (p. 13).
Show that a point is not a local maximizer with an explicit feasible path along orthogonal directions on which the objective is strictly monotone (pp. 11-12).
Round approximately feasible iterates with a support threshold eps^(1/2) taken from the largest constraint violation, and prove the property you need is preserved (p. 16).
When heuristics cannot be timed on the same machine, report the community's machine-calibration benchmark (p. 20).

quotes.text: A surprising result that we will show in this section is that the optimal values of the two formulations are equal even though the feasible region of the rank-two problem is strictly larger than that of the rank-one problem.
In fact, although “escapes” were often observed in our experiments, sometimes the algorithm did fail to escape from a non-maximum stable set.
